title: Implement hub model routing table and budget intelligence advisor
description: Build a hub-level advisor that maintains a fresh local registry of available AI providers and models, maps them to classes of work, tracks confidence/cost/capacity changes over time, and guides both Octo dispatch and manual user choice. This should present dynamic advice in language users understand: not abstract benchmark jargon, but practical gestation guidance for when to use frontier, strong planner, builder, or economy models. It becomes the canonical optimization table for model selection, budget discipline, fallback routing, and longitudinal business intelligence across the wheel.
non_goals: Do not hardcode a single provider as the permanent best choice
Do not tie routing to exact model names inside every implementation lug
Do not require live network checks for correctness in v1
Do not force spoke-local Ozi to own provider intelligence

must_be_sequential: 1. Define the hub provider/model inventory schema and source-of-truth location.
2. Define work classes (big_think, planning, coding, refactoring, verification, etc.) and routing-table semantics.
3. Define fallback cascade behavior when preferred models are unavailable, rate-limited, or over budget.
4. Define confidence/history tracking so model recommendations improve over time.
5. Define budget and capacity dimensions for user-facing optimization guidance.
6. Define how Octo and users consume the routing table during dispatch and manual work selection.
7. Persist design and verification requirements in this lug before implementation begins.
can_parallelize: Draft inventory schema and work-class taxonomy in parallel
Draft confidence tracking and budget reporting in parallel

verification_requirements: Verify the hub owns the canonical provider/model registry
Verify work classes are explicit and actionable for dispatch
Verify recommendations can degrade gracefully through fallback cascades
Verify confidence/history data is designed for later business intelligence and budget guidance
Verify users can read the table to guide their own model choices, not just Octo
Verify the routing system collects broad dimensions and lets the user preference/weight them rather than forcing a narrow starter taxonomy

acceptance_tests.expected: A future implementer can map a lug or dispatch to a class-of-work and recommended model class
Preferred model, fallback chain, and downgrade behavior are all specified
Cost, confidence, capacity, and trend tracking are part of the design rather than an afterthought

review_questions: Does the routing table stay hub-local and reusable across spokes?
Are work classes specific enough to support dispatch decisions?
Is the confidence/cost history durable enough to guide future spending decisions?
Can Octo and the user both consume the same table without duplicate logic?

review_history.summary: Lug is well-formed and approvable. Hub exists at /home/mario/projects/wheelwright/hub/ so hub/model-routing/ is a valid creation target. All three target files (registry.json, work-classes.json, confidence-history.jsonl) are concrete file paths. Inventory schema fields are fully enumerated in hub_model_registry and provider_monitoring_dimensions. Work classes are named and example-mapped in dynamic_advice_model. Fallback cascade behavior is described in sequence step 3 and verification_requirements. Routing fields (recommended_model_class, preferred_provider_model, fallback_chain, etc.) are explicit. Confidence tiers are named (preview/low/med/high). Both Octo and manual users are addressed in integration_contract. Budget/confidence tracking are durable data fields in history_fields. All ready_to_build_gate checks pass. Only one minor gap: hub/model-routing/registry.json and work-classes.json are named but their JSON structure (top-level keys, array vs map) is not fully specified — a builder should infer from inventory_fields and routing_fields listed in hub_model_registry. Acceptable at this planning level; does not block build.
recommendations: Builder should treat hub_model_registry.inventory_fields as the top-level array schema for registry.json and hub_model_registry.routing_fields as the work-classes.json entry shape.
Clarify whether confidence-history.jsonl is appended per dispatch event or per batch — JSONL append pattern is implied but not stated.
The custom_grabbers_required=true note in data_collection_requirements is a future flag; builder should scaffold the pluggable collection layer stub rather than skipping it entirely.

workflow.handoff_reason: Implementer review passed. Builder can claim.

preference_model.principle: Collect broad provider/model dimensions once, then let the user express preferences and weighting rather than constraining advice to a small starter list.

integration_contract.avoids: hardcoding exact model names into every implementation lug
integration_contract.guidance: Implementation lugs should reference work class or model class; the hub registry resolves to actual models.

notes: Refined to serve as the canonical model recommendation table for both automation and manual operator guidance.
Formalized work-class + confidence-tier guidance and provider telemetry dimensions; users should see recommendations in practical language rather than abstract benchmark jargon.
Expanded from starter-list advice to preference-weighted guidance over a richer provider/model dimension set.

checks: Hub-owned provider/model inventory path is explicit
Work classes and fallback routing are explicit
Both Octo and manual users can consume the same table
Budget/confidence tracking is designed as durable data, not chat memory

ready_to_build: Are inventory schema, routing schema, and history schema concrete enough to implement?

acceptance_checks.question: Is the hub model-routing table specific enough to drive dispatch?
acceptance_checks.pass_condition: Provider inventory, work classes, fallback chain, and confidence fields are all durable
acceptance_checks.failure_action: Return to planning and add missing fields

dynamic_advice_model.principle: Work class and confidence tier are separate axes. Work class says what kind of thinking is needed; confidence tier says how much strength or spend to buy.

work_class_examples.big_think: highest reasoning work: architecture, semantic reconciliation, deep design, subtle verification
work_class_examples.planning: structured decomposition, implementation planning, taxonomy/schema drafting
work_class_examples.coding: normal implementation work with clear targets
work_class_examples.verification: skeptical review, acceptance checks, contract validation
work_class_examples.bug_hunt: debugging; can range from builder-grade to frontier depending on subtlety

confidence_tier_examples.preview: cheap probe or rough direction, not trusted for final execution
confidence_tier_examples.low: bounded/simple work where failure cost is low and verification is easy
confidence_tier_examples.med: normal production work with verification after execution
confidence_tier_examples.high: expensive, careful, high-confidence work such as architecture or critical verification

dynamic_advice_model.user_language: Show recommendations in practical language users understand, such as when Haiku/economy class is appropriate because the problem is already made easy by decomposition.

data_collection_requirements.note: Provider-specific collectors will be needed to gather availability, limits, usage, and spend details from each service. This should be designed as a pluggable collection layer rather than hardcoded one-off scripts.
collection_sources: account usage pages where APIs are missing
data_collection_requirements.future_feature_boundary: Cross-user cohort intelligence / HIVE MIND belongs to a later networked feature, not this batch.

usage_guidance_examples.when_to_use_economy_builder: Use Haiku/economy class when the task is narrow, well decomposed, easy to verify, and failure cost is low.
usage_guidance_examples.when_not_to_use_economy_builder: Avoid Haiku/economy class for new architecture, migration contracts, subtle debugging, or ambiguous verification work.
usage_guidance_examples.historical_reframe: Using frontier models for difficult work was not wrong; the opportunity is to reduce uniform overuse by matching model strength to decomposed task shape.
